heading: Oracle Limitations, Open Problems
section_text:
Can quantum computers solve {{formula:2de743ab-f30f-4f20-85d1-cba9cc2299f0}} -complete problems in polynomial
time?  In the early days of quantum computing, Bennett et al. {{cite:5a0a45badcd919053d8a7a3922bd95e2fdb29e2d}} gave an oracle relative to which {{formula:a65f7339-f8b9-49d2-b9ed-ff373112a988}} ,
providing what is still the best evidence we have that the answer is no.  It
is easy to extend Bennett et al.'s result to give an oracle relative to which
{{formula:7de710c4-f088-4bbe-94bc-3393b935d9d6}} ; that is, {{formula:0feaf9aa-32ae-404f-8389-b73f910adf64}}  is hard
even for nonuniform quantum algorithms.  But when we try to show
{{formula:9e42b679-736c-4860-8a4a-a21221c28022}}  relative to an oracle, a new
difficulty arises: even if the oracle encodes {{formula:408e632b-a4bb-4177-9eb9-213f2f60a6c8}}  exponentially hard
search problems for each input length {{formula:e96c9337-84d0-448b-9d47-366ce5b41a60}} , the quantum advice, being an
“exponentially large object” itself, might
somehow encode information about all {{formula:5d9acaa0-a933-44cf-8bd8-aab0b7b2cc3d}}  problems.  We need to argue that
even if so, only a miniscule fraction of that information can be extracted by
measuring the advice.

How does one prove such a statement?  As it turns out, the task can be
reduced to proving a direct product theorem for quantum search.
 This is a theorem that in its weakest form says the following: given {{formula:c37bfeab-2a71-42c3-8f97-cc4f823b890b}} 
items, {{formula:1467963e-0e68-4009-b1c0-9f0441ba0340}}  of which are marked, if we lack enough time to find even
one marked item, then the probability of finding all {{formula:c2998e87-2e90-451c-9291-f66c990a603e}}  items
decreases exponentially in {{formula:4c8dea66-959c-423d-a6cf-3c7cec8bd41a}} .  For intuitively, suppose there were a
quantum advice state that let us efficiently find any one of {{formula:7fa376b9-b0b3-4d65-853a-15c8751f69ed}}  marked items.
 Then by “guessing” the advice (i.e.
replacing it by a maximally mixed state), and then using the guessed advice
multiple times, we could efficiently find all {{formula:df1649a1-4fe3-4589-8cd9-10d26f7ff23f}}  of the items with a success
probability that our direct product theorem shows is impossible.  This
reduction is formalized in Theorem REF .

But what about the direct product theorem itself?  It seems like it should be
trivial to prove—for surely there are no devious correlations by which
success in finding one marked item leads to success in finding all the others!
 So it is surprising that even a weak direct product theorem eluded proof for
years.  In 2001, Klauck {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} gave an attempted proof using the
hybrid method of Bennett et al. {{cite:5a0a45badcd919053d8a7a3922bd95e2fdb29e2d}}.  His motivation was to show a
limitation of space-bounded quantum sorting algorithms.  Unfortunately,
Klauck's proof is fallacious.Specifically, the last sentence in the
proof of Lemma 5 in {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} (“Clearly this
probability is at least {{formula:ec55e323-51e0-41ba-a80f-92031d5f9f3c}} ”) is not justified by what precedes it.

In this section we give the first correct proof of a direct product theorem,
based on the polynomial method of Beals et al. {{cite:2ff31b7d2c85795fb7aa3a59f30e11016425df62}}.  Besides showing
that {{formula:5917a3d5-d354-45bc-955c-79829cc2f6d3}}  relative to an oracle, our
result can be used to recover the conclusions in {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} about the
hardness of quantum sorting (see Klauck, Špalek, and de Wolf
{{cite:06463ca2447dbe41a8c68e403f92ac00ac00372c}} for details).  We expect the result to have other applications as well.

We will need the following lemma of Beals et al. {{cite:2ff31b7d2c85795fb7aa3a59f30e11016425df62}}, which builds
on ideas due to Minsky and Papert {{cite:e80b0fcf434d4fc9e8b162616c52f3ba69e7c91f}} and Nisan and Szegedy {{cite:725054b550aab0096c88e39fa7821f9b35461194}}.

When proving a direct product theorem, we can no longer apply Theorem
REF  so straightforwardly.  The reason is that the success
probabilities in question are extremely small, and therefore the maximum
derivative {{formula:9ad4f834-495d-420b-95e0-99501ad55bf7}}  could also be extremely small.
 Fortunately, though, we can still prove a good lower bound on the degree of
the relevant polynomial {{formula:360beb14-bb4d-4278-ac30-4e253a275920}} .  The key is to look not just at the first
derivative of {{formula:a2bccabb-28ec-4dc9-b8fd-bc33e7e941da}} , but at higher derivatives.

heading: Conclusion and Future Work
section_text:
This paper has considered bin-buffering algorithms and showed that using
a hierarchical approach, highly scalable algebraic queries were possible
even with a small buffer. Using overlapped bins, we have shown that
we could buffer several local moments simultaneously and use
much less storage than wavelet-based approaches while still supporting
progressive queries and very scalable queries and updates.

In short, we showed that {{formula:beb28896-8869-4852-86b6-6634bb8f6571}}  local moments could be buffered using
only a single real-valued buffer: using bins of a fixed size irrespective
of {{formula:da296d68-b55a-4f67-89d0-27f235a52e9c}} . Other
types of range queries could also be grouped and buffered
efficiently together {{cite:3ef5da4a02bb793893168133bd5a62bb433cc576}}.
By a direct product {{cite:aa49b595a8cf654ccc092582befe47263fd8efa8}}, Hierarchical Bin Buffering
and therefore the Ola approach
can be generalized to the multidimensional case.

Some implementation issues were not addressed. For example,
many forms of buffering using finite-accuracy floating-point numbers
are susceptible to significant numerical errors.

Finally,
the source code used for the production of this paper is freely available {{cite:cdac3b577396445090fa52fc9f277b0d703ee418}}.

heading: Conclusion and future work
section_text: In this paper the problem of synchronizing a network of identical linear systems described by the state-space model {{formula:a7e02dba-0c59-4950-b1eb-3578a5ae1f0b}}  under general interconnection topologies has been addressed. A dynamic controller ensuring exponential convergence of the solutions to a synchronized solution of the decoupled systems is provided assuming that (i) {{formula:f8589f9c-0c74-4e77-bd76-f907131ea839}}  has no exponentially unstable mode, (ii) {{formula:3ffec993-9346-4607-a733-ad410a92ac39}}  is stabilizable and {{formula:7d289923-8c74-497a-81af-4b66f95f6eb7}}  is detectable, and (iii) the communication graph is uniformly connected. Stronger conditions are shown to be sufficient (and, to some extent, also necessary) to ensure synchronization with the often considered static diffusive output coupling. The extension of the proposed technique for synchronization of nonlinear systems is the subject of ongoing work.

heading: Open questions. Conclusions
section_text:
As we have demonstrated above, different approaches to magnetic
degrees of freedom converge to a common and highly non-trivial
picture. In particular, the dual models {{cite:3dd807e682855f5073210076196a2bf29e5bd9b8}}
relate percolation of the magnetic strings to the prediction
that
they should carry density of the topological charge.
The surface operators {{cite:c5aa06e43ea80edae0ed2b80599f26c1330c658a}} provide us with an adequate
construct to describe such surfaces endowed with both gauge fields and their
duals. On the lattice, one does observe percolating surfaces, with tension
in physical units and endowed with topological charge.

In this note we emphasized that the monopole mechanism of
confinement, whatever it means in detail, assumes significant role
to be played by singular non-Abelian fields. Indeed, 'electric'
degrees of freedom are introduced directly in the Lagrangian, while
'magnetic degrees of freedom' are emerging through violations of
Bianchi identities. Hence magnetic degrees of freedom are associated
with singular fields.

The construction is well understood and known since long
{{cite:a44616aff4062335e39e1da9b50099b58cb9124f}} in the Abelian case. One can either start with a
gauge field plus a scalar, Higgs field, or one can start with pure
gauge field but admit singular field configurations, monopoles. Then
these singular fields, or defects can be traded for a scalar field
and one comes back to an effective Higgs-like formulation.

In the non-Abelian case monopoles, or 1d defects do not match the
group structure {{cite:e86ca0cbb7c1500de3def195457c9355a62458b7}}, {{cite:81d53e3a9ed3da25c04c6033b98a5270a6afb4f3}}. Instead, one should look for
classification of singular fields consistent with the non-Abelian
symmetry. As is argued in fact recently {{cite:c5aa06e43ea80edae0ed2b80599f26c1330c658a}} such defects
are 2d dimensional surfaces with non-Abelian fields living on
them. In other words, the surfaces are endowed with densities of
action and of topological charge. We argued that such surfaces can be
profiled by 1d defects, or non-Abelian monopoles, whose field is not
spherically symmetric but rather line-like.

For the defects to become dynamical degrees of freedom there should
be a fine tuning which allows infrared and ultraviolet scales to
coexist. Such fine tuning is well understood in the Abelian case,
(see Eq. (REF )). A central point: for the
dual-superconductor mechanism of confinement to be relevant, similar
fine tuning should be realized in the non-Abelian case as well. This
time, however, it is self-tuning between the action and entropy of
the 2d surfaces. No explicit form of the fine tuning is known
theoretically but coexistence of the two scale is seen in the
lattice simulations.

Also, there should be consistency between dynamics in four
dimensions, or of the original Yang-Mills fields and dynamics on the
defects world-sheet. Let us conclude with an example of such a
consistency check. For dynamics of a particle (or 1d defect) to be
in fact independent on the ultraviolet scale the action associated
with the 'monopoles' should be approximately
{{formula:91b95a3b-bc67-490e-b6cf-f6899af3b929}}

see Eq. (REF ). And this has been checked on the lattice
{{cite:413a26e8015522e476bfb548de5c35df3fa878d4}}. On the other hand, the radiative mass
(REF ) is associated now with the non-Abelian fields
which live not in the bulk but on the world-sheet (see discussion
above). Which seems to be also true on the lattice, for references
and review see {{cite:52306a6f3f8d2b4ad6d3684e31ae66036b171545}}. The condition (REF )
replaces the quantization condition for the magnetic field in case
of the non-Abelian monopoles living on the surfaces.

heading: Limitations of the Calculations
section_text:
In previous papers, we have described limitations to multiannulus
{{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}}, {{cite:8c63e70eaf872a2de8010a0826e05b4630c96625}} and single annulus
{{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}} coagulation calculations. Here, we review
how several of these limitations affect results for the simulations
described above.

As long as the statistical assumptions underlying the formalism are
met, coagulation calculations provide a reasonable representation of
real collision evolution
{{cite:5236f64017cd2f1c1db97fb6ec2df7ae8ea463d8}}, {{cite:2c64bf6c69e65cb2071f345755326f7896f1aad9}}, {{cite:dd0e5aa3e6d0aa096049e9843835c0f7712906ba}}, {{cite:a2ed2e2f74c181b1efd0087c9b099d945eb86008}}, {{cite:ef113e1b2a6ed7224b5a09878eac5b9dfb8ee795}}, {{cite:b093907d4a3cb5b9dff5174e7820be0800b942b5}}, {{cite:e05b94b0abb0e87284463403d1e211fddb97a564}}, {{cite:c46d22644756616786816ff8243f85a3ef116ca1}}, {{cite:ce9f8737a1f81a7e452b2d91c706364bba394ee4}}, {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}}, {{cite:33dddbfee7450dac3fbefd374b8812b721c5c482}}.
For calculations at 30–150 AU around 1–3 M{{formula:bbc857ae-465e-439d-b410-ab04ee1aba90}}  stars, the spacing
of mass bins in an annulus and the spacing of annuli in the disk limit
the accuracy of the results. Our standard mass spacing, {{formula:70fc209f-d068-432c-b33c-7b139dface75}} ,
lengthens the evolution time by 10% to 20% relative to more accurate
calculations with {{formula:257ac13a-028c-45b4-bbfb-2acd3023d202}}  1.4 {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}}. The radial resolution, {{formula:50ffe053-2d66-4894-b232-762e76852b57}}  = 0.025, also
lengthens the evolution time. Compared to calculations described in
{{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}, improvements in our treatment of interactions among
particles in neighboring annuli reduce lags by a factor of two,
from {{formula:120b00dc-7c7d-489a-a616-7bc9090105e7}}  20% to {{formula:08a08372-60a3-413c-84e4-1c539fc1d85f}}  10%. Combining the lags for mass
spacing and radial resolution, our evolution timescales are {{formula:f02c34c8-781d-4e41-b7a2-cfc29235d6dd}} 
20% to 30% longer than the actual evolution times. This lag is
comparable to the dispersion in timescales derived from multiple
calculations with identical starting conditions. Thus, improvements
in resolution are unlikely to alter our results significantly.

heading: Future Work
section_text:
This paper has provided a preliminary exploration of metadata generation in terms of metadata property propagation within an associative network of repository resources. Further research in this area may prove useful for other network types such as those generated from other metadata properties. For instance, it may be of interest to study the effect of this algorithm on usage networks {{cite:468a23a878b132724286a69804c9d8374e3227f1}}. Usage metadata, unlike citation and journal metadata, is applicable to every accessible resource. It would be interesting to see what co-usage means for a particular genera of resources by determining which metadata properties these networks are best at propagating.

A variety of propagation algorithms may also be explored. It is assumed that a particle will take only edges of a particular {{formula:69034a93-9efc-465a-822a-5a926b5ed2be}}  type for the duration of their life-span. Different path types might be an important aspect of increasing the precision and recall performance of this method. For instance, keyword metadata that first propagates over co-authorship edges and then over co-citation edges might provide better results. Methods to implement such propagation algorithms have been presented in {{cite:0fc36c236f0c23307785f02f30afb7c963cc9968}}, {{cite:ac83c19a43bc3812eb92d333a562fe90717a74f2}}. Also, different edge types can be merged such that all co-keyword and co-authorship edges are collapsed to form a single edge.

What has been presented in this study is the results of this algorithm without the intervention of any human components (besides the initial creation of metadata through the hep-th dataset creation process). Future work that studies this method with the inclusion of humans that help to validate and “clean" the recommended metadata would be telling of how much this method is able to speed up the process of generating accurate and reliable metadata for metadata-poor resources. Such an analysis is left to future research.

Finally, multiplicative effects due to particle interaction may effect the results of the algorithm. For instance, if two particles, {{formula:259b42d2-baa5-450b-b757-10dec3ad9808}}  and {{formula:6bc0533a-75fe-4e38-811f-39afda2f9096}} , meet at a particular node, {{formula:ce269697-9b00-45cc-853f-a1ecda243696}} , and {{formula:b85f1c22-1d44-44b3-ae8c-cc1e2f6946f8}}  and {{formula:ad79b342-7582-4f30-9ed8-c6bf27d05b3a}}  have similar metadata then the footprint they leave at {{formula:eabf6d95-a9d8-4b7e-a89b-774502603579}}  should be more noticeable. Because two different metadata sources are supplying the same property values, there is an increased probability of that recommended metadata value being correct. Currently, only a summation is being provided. It may be interesting to multiply this summation by the number of unique particles that provided energy for a particular recommended metadata value. The variations of this preliminary framework will be explored in future work.

heading: Open problems
section_text:
Study the structure of the graph {{formula:3fd1f3fd-6f2b-494c-a68e-b60e5651f84f}} . Determine if it belongs to a family of connected graphs arising from {{formula:da7b5e4b-78c4-4614-ba1d-b7fc97bdaef4}} , having an infinite number of members, as it is for the graphs arising from {{formula:c2d33c5b-9b43-423f-a9f8-c0ac37d2bcab}} .

Since there is no general classification of weighing matrices, characterizing graphs of Hankel weighing matrices seems to be out of reach. This could be however done for graphs of degree 4 and 9, on the basis of present knowledge on {{formula:d4a6afcf-30a2-472b-8737-06b8e9fb234c}}  and {{formula:3ebada2b-1957-4fef-bfde-668b53de2673}}  (see {{cite:d2b81348ac8204edd98e7fd48d8bb1df5c9ba744}}).

We have seen that there are examples of Hankel weighing matrices which are not anticirculant. A way to study the relation between these matrices and anticirculant ones, would be to prove that the graphs of Hankel weighing matrices are always isomorphic to graphs of {{formula:f1f125b5-a07c-4699-96d3-b7290f902bfa}} , except for some special cases which will include the examples in proposition REF .
{{figure:40a0d05d-9172-4b05-8a9d-7c2ecdd1f0cb}}
A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is an ordered set of sequentially adjacent vertices, in which every vertex of the graph appears exactly once. Graphs with Hamiltonian cycles are said to be Hamiltonian. Alspach and Zhang {{cite:23331cfdeb1acc1bf9b321884f681030ecb73bf7}} conjectured that a connected Cayley graph {{formula:2861b017-0d38-45fa-995f-f397d0e45869}}  is Hamiltonian whenever {{formula:b41dad51-c21f-4a9f-bf1b-a6f38a52efc4}}  is a set of reflections. According to this conjecture, any connected anticirculant graph is Hamiltonian whenever it is loopless. Additionally, Gutin et al.  {{cite:277f0406c3fc7217d6eea449d5b4ffc473ba8b53}} conjectured that graphs of unitary matrices are Hamiltonian if connected. According to these conjectures the graphs of Hankel weighing matrices are Hamiltonian if connected. This is the case for the graphs considered here. In Figure REF  are drawn the graphs {{formula:1bb5c92d-9485-4a4f-8aab-5e93c85e4aac}}  and {{formula:9c17e54d-f301-4679-9f48-6674a17810f9}} . The highlighted edges represent Hamiltonian cycles. Perhaps the physical picture that motivates our study could provide some insight toward proving these conjectures.

We have seen that graphs of the form {{formula:67564a15-6a2b-4b87-aebd-d4329fbe44a8}}  are graphs of unitary matrices. The quantum dynamics induced by these matrices is trivial because of symmetry. However symmetry can be broken with the action of a diagonal matrix without altering the zero pattern of the unitary. This suggests the possibility of constructing unitaries with a nontrivial dynamics whose graph is a undirected Cayley graph of the dihedral group.

Sections  and  make extensive use of the following trick. Begin with a circulant weighing matrix, then reverse the columns. If the resulting graph has loops, one can create a loopless graph by the “interlacing” trick. In fact the interlaced graph will again be connected if the original graph was connected but not bipartite. Can one classify the Hankel and anticirculant weighing matrices which cannot be obtained by this trick?

heading: Improvements and Future Work
section_text:
With several methods for age-dating brown dwarfs over a broad range of phase space now
available,
opportunities to use these objects as chronometers for various
Galactic studies look to be increasingly promising; e.g., age-dating
planetary systems, examining cluster age spreads,
testing Galactic disk dynamical heating models, and direct measures of the
substellar mass function and birthrate in the field and other populations. However, there are areas where improvements
in uncertainties are needed and basic assumptions tested. Surface gravity determinations
in particular require better constraints, since these
enable age-dating of individual sources. In the short term, improvements
in spectral models can help in this endeavor; however, a sufficiently sampled grid of
benchmark sources
may obviate the need for models entirely.
Benchmarks should increasingly arise from mass standards, for which
age constraints are more precise; these additionally provide
necessary tests of evolutionary models upon which most of the age-dating
techniques hinge. Improved angular resolution and sensitivity
with {{formula:c355ace2-97f7-441c-892b-5b9952550f3e}}  and the next generation of large ({{formula:ea7f78cb-378b-4c98-acd2-38b0a459a0c8}} m) telescopes
will increase resolved binary sample sizes by expanding the volume in which they
can be found and monitored. These facilities will also aid searches for
substellar cluster members in old open field and globular clusters and, perhaps more
importantly, mass standards in these clusters to facilitate more stringent tests of evolutionary models
(T. Dupuy, priv. comm.).
Finally, a larger, more complete sample of brown dwarfs with precise RV measurements
will both improve our statistical constraints on the age of the local brown dwarf
population (and subpopulations) while additionally aiding in the search for mass standards.

The author thanks T. Dupuy, S. Leggett, M. Liu, & A. West for helpful comments.

heading: Conclusion and Open Problems
section_text:
We studied the matroid isomorphism problem under various input
representations and restriction on the rank of the matroid. We proved
that graph isomorphism,
graphic matroid isomorphism and bounded rank version of matroid isomorphism
are all polynomial time equivalent.

In addition, we find it interesting that in the bounded rank case,
{{formula:67e88915-6dab-467c-86b3-9ecc39083464}}  and {{formula:73a9eab3-bef5-4755-b312-be18f0212e9c}}  are equivalent, though there exist matroids of
bounded rank which are not representable over any field. Some of the
open questions that we see are as follows:

Our results provide new possibilities to attack the graph
isomorphism problem. For example, it will be interesting to prove a
{{formula:bf11a214-943f-4bd0-8256-01184643d69f}}  upper bound for {{formula:a565f4cf-3afd-445c-80fc-35aac302745d}} . Note that this will imply that

{{formula:b1bc22ba-5df9-41e0-af2d-0e0e2806e501}}  (other than what is translated from the bounds for {{formula:66119676-2026-470d-ad92-ecc2591db094}} )
which can be solved in polynomial time?

The representations of the matroid in the definition of {{formula:0e5247ae-769f-42ec-88f9-6256404ec067}} 
is over fields of size at least {{formula:fd9e4674-c05f-4b5d-8f5f-4ad51bcf12f1}}  and at most {{formula:5f94f549-04f2-4d28-969a-d2893ccbca5c}} , where
{{formula:d54f65eb-9d58-468b-b3ac-c541902d1fc5}}  is the size of the ground set of the matroid. This is critically
needed for the observation of {{formula:ed4610c8-dc2d-439e-a414-b855faf3ac0c}} -hardness. One could ask if
the problem is easier over fixed finite fields independent on the
input. However, we note that, by our results, it follows that this
problem over {{formula:d69eaf44-6579-410a-9109-f46d53a58f46}}  is already hard for {{formula:cc8ebbbd-ccaf-4230-89d7-398a70b7caa3}} . It will still be
interesting to give a better (than the trivial {{formula:13fc76b0-a8a2-468c-86b2-d1f810e3e58f}} ) upper
bound for linear matroids represented over fixed finite fields (even
for {{formula:e44a632e-ecf4-4a9b-891a-951b45448747}} ).

Can we use the colouring technique of linear matroid isomorphism
to reduce the general instances of linear matroid isomorphism to
isomorphism testing of “simpler components” of the matroid?

Can we make the reduction from {{formula:3a57d6cb-005e-4e6a-8cb9-22de9d9fdbb8}}  to {{formula:14b40ab7-67b3-4493-8c98-b150b4fc9983}}  many-one? Can we
improve the complexity of this reduction in the general case?
